name: Teleport
summary: The unit vanishes from one spot and appears at another without crossing the ground between: walls, cliffs, water and enemy lines don't matter. Short versions are an instant hop on a short cooldown or a few charges, used to dodge, chase or slip behind a target. Long versions reach any spot the unit can see, but pay for it with a long recharge, a large energy cost or a dangerous arrival, where the unit stands frozen and exposed for longer the farther it jumped. Some versions jump to a marker or a projected image the unit sent ahead, or back to a fixed friendly point, and some move teammates instead of the user. Teleporting moves the unit within the fight; arriving on the battlefield is a separate pattern, drop in from above.
counterplay: Watch the tell: a marker, an image sent ahead, a charge display or a flash at the departure point gives the destination away.
Punish the arrival: area fire or a waiting group catches a long-range jumper while it phases in, unable to move or fire.
Bait out the jump, then fight it while it recharges; with no charges left it can't escape.
Silence or root it: effects that block abilities strand it where it last landed.
Shoot or guard the marker in beacon versions; damaging it can kill the user who jumps to it.
Keep long-range and support units guarded, since they are the usual targets of a jump.

other_examples.note: Once its device is fully charged, the tank can shift itself to any point its side can see and stays there, with no automatic return; it then recharges before the next jump. It is fragile for its price, so it is used for hit-and-run raids, such as jumping into a base to knock out its power.

sources.title: Chrono tank (Aftermath), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Quotes the unit's entry in the Aftermath manual.

other_examples.note: Drives out to the ore like any vehicle, but teleports straight back to its refinery when full, and can be ordered to do so to escape an attack. The jump leaves an infesting drone behind.

sources.title: Chrono Miner, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Quotes the unit's entry in the Red Alert 2 manual.

other_examples.note: Two friendly units trade places, which brings a slow unit to the front at once. Both are disabled and open to attack after the swap, for longer the farther apart they were, and a unit swapped into terrain it can't survive in is lost.

A researched ability: an instant short teleport on a short cooldown that needs sight of the destination and ignores cliffs. Players use it to ambush, catch fleeing units or get out of a losing fight; a rooting spell blocks it.

Sends out a shade that can't be hurt and can walk but not fight; a few seconds later the adept jumps to wherever the shade has got to, unless the player cancels it first. Good for scouting and for getting around defences.
Pulls a group of friendly units from a chosen area to the arbiter's own position, which can take them straight into an enemy base past its defences.

sources.title: Arbiter (StarCraft), StarCraft Wiki
sources.note: Its overview names the raid use: recalling an army into an enemy base around its defences.

other_examples.unit: Aeon Armored Command Unit (Personal Teleporter enhancement)
other_examples.note: A bought upgrade that lets the commander teleport anywhere on the map, at a huge energy cost per jump, so it is a late-game move.

sources.title: Aeon Armored Command Unit, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.note: An infantry squad that jumps through the warp to a chosen spot. A full charge holds two jumps, and an empty one takes a long time to refill.

sources.title: Dawn of War/Warp Spider Squad, Dawn of War Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: A short instant hop in the direction the hero is moving, with three stored charges that come back every few seconds; she chains them to cross gaps, flank and dodge. A hindering status effect blocks it.
A beacon: first it was placed so the hero could jump back to it while it lasted, later thrown ahead of her for a short-range teleport. Enemies can follow the light trail she leaves.

sources.title: Tracer, Overwatch Wiki
sources.note: Its matchup tips mention following Sombra's light trail after a translocation.

shooter_analogues.note: Primary fire throws a disc, secondary fire teleports the player to it. Landing on an enemy kills them; enemies can shoot the disc, and jumping to a damaged disc kills the user; a flag carrier who teleports drops the flag. Later games limit it with charges that refill slowly.

player_translation.summary: Press Space to vanish and reappear a short way off, through walls and over gaps. The long-range version lets you pick any spot you can see, but you arrive frozen for a moment, longer the farther you went, so the enemy can punish a careless jump.
as_user: You pick fights on your terms: hop behind a slow tank, onto a sniper's ledge or across a river, then hop out before the enemy turns.
Every jump is a decision: spend a charge to engage and you have one less to escape.
Long jumps are a gamble: you cross half the map at once, but arrive helpless for a moment, so short hops are safer than one big one.
Beacon and recall versions let you plan ahead: send a marker to a flank, then jump when the fight turns.
as_target: A flash at the start point and a marker or flicker at the landing point tell you where it went, so you can turn and fire.
If it lands frozen, that is your window: everything you have on the arrival point.
Once it has used its charges it is just a fragile unit; count the jumps and push when it's out.
In beacon versions, shoot the marker or wait beside it.
teammates: Recall and swap variants move teammates: pull your squad to a flank, or trade places with a slow ally to bring them to the front.
A teleporter makes a good bait: it draws fire, then vanishes, so teammates can punish enemies who chased it.
Defenders guard their long-range and support players, who are what a jump usually aims at.
controls: Space (key-bound movement): tap to blink a short way along your current movement, or toward the cursor when standing still.
Long-jump variant: hold Space to show a landing marker under the cursor, release to jump, right mouse to cancel; a short phase-in follows.
Beacon variant: tap Space to throw the marker, tap again to jump to it; hold Space to recall the marker.
Recall and swap variants: Q on a teammate or an area; teammates see a countdown and can step out of the area to refuse.
feedback: A bright departure flash and a matching arrival flash, both visible from above, with a faint line between them for a moment.
A landing marker shown to enemies a split second before arrival for long jumps, and a frozen, flickering outline while phasing in.
Charge pips under the unit's health bar that enemies can read.
A clear 'blocked' cue when a jump is denied by a silence or an invalid destination.
changes_from_rts: In the source unit the ordinary move order teleports; a player needs the jump on its own key, with a clear destination marker, so walking and jumping stay separate.
Map-wide jumps on a click are too strong in a shooter; long range needs a long recharge, a visible destination and a frozen arrival.
Destination checks must stop players from jumping into sealed rooms, out of the map or inside other units; a telefrag only happens where a variant allows it.
Objective carriers drop what they carry when they teleport, as Unreal Tournament flag carriers do, so a jump can't skip the objective.
Red Alert's Chronosphere kills ordinary soldiers it moves, and Red Alert 3's Chrono Swap destroys units moved into terrain they can't survive in; here an invalid destination simply refuses the jump.

team_play.notes: Mostly a personal skill tool, but recall and swap variants move teammates, a beacon or projected image scouts ahead for the team, and a teleporter makes good bait that pulls enemies into its team's fire.

notes: Instant position changes need server-side destination checks (walkable ground, no walls, no other units, inside the map) and lag-tolerant correction so the jump never rubber-bands.
Long-jump variants need a phase-in state in which the unit can't move or fire but can be hurt, with its time scaled by distance.
Beacon variants need a throwable, destructible marker with its own physics.
Recall and swap variants move other players, which needs their consent rules and the same destination checks for everyone moved.
Many systems must react to a jump: attached infesters, tethers and beams, objective carrying, seat and vehicle states.
Free escape makes a unit impossible to finish; charges and recharge times are the main levers.
Long jumps onto backline players can feel unfair without a warning at the landing point.
Teleporting past chokepoints or onto objectives can skip whole map designs.
Moving teammates (recall, swap) multiplies the effect on the fight.
From a top-down camera a unit that vanishes is easy to lose; departure and arrival need matching, bright effects.
Several teleporters jumping at once make the screen hard to read.
Players need to tell a short blink from a long jump at a glance, since the arrival risk differs.

variants.name: Short blink
variants.summary: An instant short hop toward where the unit is moving or aiming, from a few charges that refill over a few seconds or on a short cooldown; it needs a clear landing spot.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Stalker Blink; Overwatch Tracer's Blink

variants.name: Long jump, frozen arrival
variants.summary: Jump to any spot you can see, but arrive frozen and exposed for longer the farther you went, so several short hops are safer than one long one.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Chrono Legionnaire and Chrono Commando; Red Alert 3 Chrono Swap

adds_weaknesses.why: After every jump it stands frozen and open to fire, longer the farther it went, unable to move or shoot.

variants.name: Charged shift
variants.summary: A long recharge, or a large energy cost, buys one jump to anywhere in sight; the unit stays where it lands, with no way back until it recharges.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert: The Aftermath Chrono Tank; Supreme Commander commander teleporter

variants.name: Beacon jump
variants.summary: Throw or place a marker, then teleport to it while it lasts. Enemies can see it, shoot it or wait beside it, and a damaged marker kills whoever jumps to it.
variants.seen_in: Unreal Tournament Translocator; Overwatch Sombra's Translocator

variants.name: Jump home
variants.summary: Teleport back to a fixed friendly point, such as a spawn, a depot or a deployed beacon, to escape or to deliver cargo; elsewhere the unit has to travel normally.

adds_strengths.why: Gets back to a fixed friendly point in an instant from anywhere, to escape a losing fight or to bring cargo home without the trip.

variants.name: Send an image ahead
variants.summary: Project an untouchable image that walks ahead and scouts; after a short delay you swap to its position, unless you cancel. Enemies see the image coming and know where you will appear.

variants.name: Recall or swap teammates
variants.summary: Pull nearby teammates to your position after a short countdown, or trade places with one ally; whoever is moved arrives briefly disabled.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft Arbiter Recall; Red Alert 3 Chrono Swap

adds_strengths.why: Can bring teammates to a flank or a slow ally to the front in an instant.

variants.name: Never walks
variants.summary: The unit has no ordinary movement: every move is a teleport to the spot clicked, each followed by a phase-in that grows with distance.

adds_weaknesses.why: Can't walk at all; every move ends in a frozen phase-in where it is helpless.

adds_strengths.why: Crosses walls, gaps and front lines in an instant, to flank, chase or escape.

adds_weaknesses.why: Each jump has a tell and a recharge; caught with no charges left, it has no way out.

counters.why: Jumps past the escorts onto artillery and other long-range units that can't defend themselves up close.

countered_by.why: Blocking its abilities strands it wherever it last landed.
Area fire on the landing spot catches it as it arrives, and the arrival flash gives that spot away.

open_questions: On a card, the teleport mobility trait already uses a key (Space) and stands for this pattern. Should the pattern ever appear as a separate ability, or only through the trait, so the key is counted once?
May a teleport pass through enemy-only walls and shields, or only terrain? (Recommended: terrain and friendly obstacles only.)
Should landing on an enemy ever kill it (telefrag), or should the jump always be refused?
Should long jumps need the destination to be in the user's own sight, or in the team's shared sight?

shooter_fit.reason: Shooters already use blinks and translocators well, and from above a jump reads as a clear flash-to-flash move; it needs strong tells and destination rules so units can't vanish from fights or skip objectives.
